description: Curated touchstone library for Conductor scripts. Source of truth. Human-editable. Migrated losslessly from the five killer-app seed pools (notes/2026-09-07-killer-app-FIVE-scripts.md, commit 82059d2). See notes/2026-09-10-touchstone-library.md for the dedupe map and tag vocabulary.

field_notes.line: Exact touchstone wording, verbatim from the seed-pool bullet (quoted phrase where the bullet quoted one, else the bullet's descriptor). Never paraphrased.
field_notes.recognition: 0-100 estimated concept-recognition. null = present in a seed pool but not plucked into a script, so never scored.
field_notes.degrades: true if the line still lands literally for people who don't hold the reference (graceful degradation).
field_notes.shaka_risk: true if recognition-dependence is high enough that a non-holder gets little/nothing (a 'shaka' miss).
field_notes.fire_as: Suggested action type; 'random' = emergent-harmony crowd murmur across phones. null = normal.

entries.notes: Meme-level even for non-viewers. Crowd-murmur staging (fired as random) is the payoff. Script renders it 'I am Spartacus.'
'FREEDOM!' is iconic; the line carries stakes literally.
Concept > attribution; the refusal reads plainly. Full line: 'mad as hell / not going to take this anymore'.

entries.line: governments should be afraid of their people
entries.notes: Strong Conductor-thesis line; V-mask cultural halo. Companion V line seeded in the demo note: 'remember the 5th of November'.
Descriptor bullet. Canonical quote: 'First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win.' Ubiquitous activist meme; carries literally regardless of attribution.

entries.line: Ye are many — they are few
entries.notes: 55% as quote / ~95% by plain sense — self-evident in a crowd; Occupy '99%' revival. Script renders the plucked form 'We are many. They are few.'
Seeded in pool 1, not plucked into a script — so never recognition-scored.
Descriptor bullet (demo note gloss: 'stayed seated'). Seeded, not plucked.
DEDUPE: appeared in pool 1 (We Are Many) AND pool 2 (The Experiment) — merged into this single multi-theme entry. Broadly known; deliberately left unfinished so the crowd fills it.
Descriptor bullet. Seeded, not plucked.

entries.line: the experiment requires that you continue
entries.notes: Cold institutional voice lands even without the name; the stat is the detonation. Companion: '37 of 40 kept going'. Shaka-adjacent but mitigated by phrasing.
Widely taught; the plucked line works with zero prior knowledge: 'Prisoner. Guard. It took six days to forget which you were.'
SHAKA-RISK. Kept only because the plucked line is fully self-contained literally: 'Which line matches? You knew. You said the wrong one anyway.'
Seeded in pool 2, not plucked.
Seeded in pool 2, not plucked.
Seeded in pool 2, not plucked.
Gloss: enemies unite vs. a common foe. ~35-50% among Trek fans, near-zero otherwise; the shape ('two must unite') still reads as sound-poetry.
Gloss: a gift, giving.
Gloss: failure, collapse. The library's namesake shaka miss; leaked widely via the famous essay/meme.
Gloss: sudden understanding.

entries.line: Darmok and Jalad on the ocean
entries.notes: Gloss: two who fought together, now bonded.

entries.line: like tears in rain / time to die
entries.notes: Meme-famous monologue.
E.T.'s glowing finger is iconic.

entries.line: Do not go gentle / rage against the dying of the light
entries.notes: The most-quoted villanelle in English; Interstellar boosted it.
Degrades perfectly: reads as a plain sigh even unplaced.

entries.line: To live in hearts we leave behind is not to die
entries.notes: Seeded in pool 4, not plucked.
The resolution line: the dead persist in the living.
Crowd is meant to yell it back; fired as random for ragged near-unison.
Deadpan comic beat.
Defiance beat.

entries.line: May the Force be with you
entries.notes: Benediction beat; highest recognition in the set.
Seeded in pool 5, not plucked.
Skews younger/online. The blowoff/release beat.
Descriptor bullet — a literal SFX punchline, not a spoken line.
Seeded in pool 5, not plucked.

entries.line: Say hello to my little friend.
entries.notes: Seeded in pool 5, not plucked.

entries.line: Frankly, my dear, I don't give a damn
entries.notes: AFI's #1 movie quote. Clark Gable as Rhett Butler. Exit-line energy.
Bogart's toast. Works as a genuine sendoff without film context.

entries.source: Apollo 13 (1995; actual NASA transmission was 'Houston, we've had a problem')
entries.notes: Film version is more iconic than the real transmission. Universal understated-crisis signal.

entries.line: You're gonna need a bigger boat
entries.notes: Understatement-of-scale meme. Works as literal advice.

entries.line: I'm the king of the world!
entries.notes: DiCaprio on the bow. As random: everyone yelling it at once.
Jack Nicholson. Truth-confrontation energy.
Dorothy's heel-click incantation. Works as pure yearning even without the context.
Haley Joel Osment. Deadpan. One of the most-quoted film lines of the late 90s.
Dory's perseverance chant. Degrades as plain 'keep going.'
Buzz Lightyear. Maximalist ambition. Great crowd-launch beat.

entries.line: Life is like a box of chocolates; you never know what you're gonna get
entries.notes: Mama's wisdom. Often shortened in culture. Works as plain philosophy.
Jenny's cry. Crowd shouting at runners is the canonical flash-mob beat.

entries.source: Dr. No (1962) and every Bond film
entries.notes: Most parodied character introduction in film history.
Schwarzenegger. Dark comic farewell. Meme-stable across decades.

entries.line: Do or do not. There is no try.
entries.source: Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1980), Yoda
entries.notes: Yoda's coaching line. Degrades as pure exhortation.

entries.source: Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1980)
entries.notes: Vader's revelation. Exact film wording; 'Luke, I am your father' is the widespread misquote.
Vulcan salutation. Works as a genuine sendoff regardless of Trek knowledge.
Ledger's Joker. Works as a pure rhetorical question.

entries.source: Return of the Jedi (1983), Admiral Ackbar
entries.notes: Internet-meme immortal. Works as a pure warning cry even without Ackbar.
MCU rally cry. Conductor is a perfect non-film context. As random it cascades.

entries.line: With great power comes great responsibility
entries.source: Spider-Man (2002; the principle predates the film)
entries.notes: Uncle Ben's mantra. Self-evident as a principle; Spider-Man association is dominant.

entries.line: I volunteer! I volunteer as tribute!
entries.notes: Katniss stepping forward. As random: multiple people volunteer at once. Protest-forward energy.

entries.source: Game of Thrones (TV, 2011–2019), House Stark motto
entries.notes: Warning-about-approaching-doom. Works as a literal portent.
Ygritte's recurring dig. Famous for calling out oblivious certainty.
Tribal affirmation. As random: crowd-ripple call-and-response. Works as pure conviction.
Clean form of McClane's catchphrase; the full line is NSFW.
Cuba Gooding Jr.'s demand. Crowd yelling it is the classic beat.

entries.line: One does not simply walk into Mordor
entries.source: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), Boromir
entries.notes: Boromir's warning, immortalized by the 'One does not simply...' meme template.

entries.line: Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country
entries.notes: JFK's defining inversion. Lands as a civic challenge without attribution.

entries.line: The only thing we have to fear is fear itself
entries.notes: Depression-era rallying cry. Works as pure anti-paralysis exhortation.

entries.line: Four score and seven years ago
entries.notes: Iconic opening; archaic '87 years ago' phrasing but universally placed.
Highest-recognition in the speeches category. Works as a plain aspiration statement.

entries.line: Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!
entries.notes: Defining Cold War demand. Even without the name it reads as a confrontation call.

entries.line: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind
entries.notes: Armstrong intended 'a man' but the 'a' was inaudible. The 'for man' version is canonical.

entries.line: Give me liberty, or give me death!
entries.notes: Revolutionary-era ultimatum. Degrades as a clean either-or choice.

entries.line: We shall fight on the beaches
entries.notes: Anchor line from Churchill's 'we shall never surrender' speech.

entries.line: I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat
entries.notes: Churchill's first speech as PM. 'Blood, sweat and tears' is the common shorthand.
The defining call to collective action. As random: each phone fires it for crowd effect.

entries.source: Julius Caesar (47 BC, after the Battle of Zela)
entries.notes: Latin: I came, I saw, I conquered. So famous even non-Latinists know the translation.
Nixon's famous denial. Irony is the payload — its literal falseness is the cultural knowledge.

entries.source: Obama 2008 presidential campaign (also United Farm Workers: 'Sí, se puede', 1972)
entries.notes: Dual roots: UFW 1972 and Obama 2008. As random it cascades into a crowd affirmation.

entries.source: protest chant (emerged 1980s, especially Howard Beach incident 1986)
entries.notes: Causality made into a rhyming demand. As random it cascades into a crowd chant.
Call-and-response protest staple. Self-evident as a territorial claim.

entries.line: The people, united, will never be defeated
entries.source: translation of 'El pueblo unido, jamás será vencido' (Sergio Ortega, Chile, 1973)
entries.notes: Global protest anthem hook. Degrades as a plain solidarity declaration.
Rhymed refusal. Template for 'X, we won't Y' chants ever since.

entries.source: civil rights anthem (from 'I'll Overcome Someday', c.1900; popularized by Pete Seeger and SNCC)
entries.notes: Global civil rights movement anchor. Works as a plain future-tense affirmation.

entries.source: United Farm Workers (Dolores Huerta and Cesar Chavez, 1972)
entries.notes: 'Yes, it can be done.' Chant root for Obama's 'Yes we can.' Both forms carry recognition.

entries.line: What do we want? [X]! When do we want it? Now!
entries.notes: The [X] slot makes it infinitely adaptable. Event script can fill the variable.

entries.source: 1960s peace movement slogan (attributed to Gerd Stern / Diane di Prima, popularized 1965)
entries.notes: Antithesis slogan. The wit survives decontextualization.

entries.source: Black Panther Party (1966); John Lennon song (1971)
entries.notes: Political slogan that crossed into pop culture via Lennon. As random: ripple-fire across phones.

entries.line: We will, we will rock you
entries.notes: The stomp-stomp-clap is inseparable from the chant; the line stands alone at any mass gathering.
Stadium singalong; cultural shorthand for perseverance. Known across age groups.

entries.line: It's the eye of the tiger
entries.notes: Rocky III anthem; pure motivation shorthand. The opening line is the touchstone.

entries.source: Livin' on a Prayer — Bon Jovi (1986)
entries.notes: Crowd singalong in the key change. The phrase signals blue-collar perseverance.

entries.source: Let It Go — Frozen (2013), sung by Idina Menzel
entries.notes: Children know every word; adults have heard it until they couldn't take it. Near-universal recognition.
Anthem of resilience; instantly recognizable even without the disco context.

entries.line: Sweet Caroline / ba-ba-ba / Good times never seemed so good
entries.notes: The 'ba-ba-ba' crowd response is a stadium ritual at Fenway and worldwide. Call-and-response staging is the payoff.

entries.source: Seven Nation Army — The White Stripes (2003)
entries.notes: Guitar riff rendered as crowd chant; the syllables are the lyric. One of the most replicated stadium chants of the 2000s.

entries.line: na na na na-na-na-na / Hey Jude
entries.notes: The coda is one of rock's great mass-participation moments; non-Beatles fans still join in.

entries.line: It's fun to stay at the YMCA
entries.notes: The arm-letter dance and chant are inseparable; near-universal recognition as a party and stadium staple.

entries.line: Is this the real life? Is this just fantasy?
entries.notes: Wayne's World cemented its mass-sing status. Opening line is the touchstone moment.
Cultural penetration across age groups; the phrase signals brush-off and resilience.
Working-class escape anthem; the phrase stands alone as aspiration and breaking free.

entries.line: Here we are now, entertain us
entries.notes: Gen X generational touchstone; sardonic crowd appeal.
Universally deployed at team celebrations and community events.
Adopted globally from Spanish football; universally legible as celebration regardless of origin.
Fundamental audience-participation call at American football and basketball games.
The syncopated clap pattern is as recognizable as the words. Fires at any mass event.
Crowd honor call; recognized even by non-sports fans.

entries.line: Na na na na, na na na na, hey hey hey, goodbye
entries.source: Na Na Hey Hey Kiss Him Goodbye — Steam (1969) / stadium tradition
entries.notes: Stadium standard for mocking the losing team; widely adopted by baseball crowds.

entries.source: You'll Never Walk Alone — Gerry and the Pacemakers (1963) / Liverpool FC anthem
entries.notes: Liverpool FC and Celtic FC crowd anthem; the phrase alone signals collective solidarity.

entries.source: University of Alabama / SEC football cheer
entries.notes: SEC football's most recognizable war cry; national prominence via college football.
One of the most recognized advertising slogans ever. Fully autonomous from brand context.

entries.line: Ba da ba ba baa — I'm lovin' it
entries.notes: The jingle hook is inseparable from the phrase; near-universal global recognition.
Became a Silicon Valley / counterculture touchstone; used ironically and sincerely.
The '[noun]?' parody template is itself a cultural artifact. Universally parodied.
80s US political/pop culture shorthand for demanding substance. Clara Peller delivered it.
One of the oldest recognized ad jingles in American culture. The three-beat rhythm is highly usable.

entries.line: Have a break, have a Kit Kat
entries.notes: UK-originated; global reach. The 'break' pun is widely appreciated.
Became a cultural meme extending far beyond candy advertising.
Moved beyond its military context into general motivation and aspiration shorthand.
Enduring idiom that escaped its advertising origin into general use.
Fred's exultant shout; pure jubilation with no semantic content. Fires as a celebration trigger.

entries.source: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1987 animated series)
entries.notes: 90s kids' shorthand for going for it. Migrated into general use as a surf/skate call.
Transformation call; recognized by 90s children globally. Shaka risk for non-viewers.

entries.source: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe (1983)
entries.notes: 80s cartoon battle cry; culturally persistent beyond the show's run. Rings as dramatic invocation even without context.
Optimus Prime's deployment command; 80s/00s crossover recognition from the live-action films.
Added to the Oxford English Dictionary. Near-universal recognition across cultures. Homer's frustrated exclamation.

entries.source: Sheldon Cooper — The Big Bang Theory (2007–2019)
entries.notes: Sheldon's prank reveal; widely known via cultural osmosis. Shaka risk for non-viewers — the word means nothing on its own.
Road Runner's escape sound; universally recognizable. Pure playground energy.
Bugs's nonchalant greeting; one of animation's most famous lines.
Classic closing line; culturally recycled as an ending signifier in any context.
Mr. Burns's scheming approval with finger-steeple; widely parodied. The word alone is legible as approval.

entries.line: To boldly go where no man has gone before
entries.source: Star Trek: The Original Series opening monologue (1966–1969)
entries.notes: Opening monologue of TOS; universally recognized as an aspiration and exploration call.

entries.source: The Borg — Star Trek: The Next Generation (1987–1994)
entries.notes: Borg collective's assimilation call; used ironically as cultural shorthand for inevitable forces.

entries.source: Jimmy Dugan — A League of Their Own (1992)
entries.notes: Tom Hanks as manager; widely recycled with any '[noun]' substitution.
Mirror monologue; cultural shorthand for challenge and confrontation. Widely parodied.

entries.source: Bill S. Preston — Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure (1989)
entries.notes: Became an internet-age kindness shorthand. Degrades perfectly — the message is its own.

entries.line: I feel the need — the need for speed!
entries.notes: Pre-flight ritual turned general enthusiasm signal. Widely parodied.
